title: Built for trust and control: Powering the next wave of AI agents across Google Workspace and Google Cloud
raw_text: For over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud. From personal and financial records to board materials, regulated workloads, applications, and AI models, those safeguards protect what matters most. Blocking >99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, alongside encryption and data residency, follows one principle: your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it. That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. More than 18 billion reads from Drive each day come from API callers. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path. Today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud. Builders get modern, agent-ready interfaces, and organizations get the visibility and control to adopt AI agents with confidence. Purpose-built interfaces: Workspace MCP servers, Workspace CLI, and Cloud Agent Gateway To help developers build reliable agents faster without forcing security teams to compromise, we are bringing agent-native interfaces to Workspace and Google Cloud: Workspace MCP servers : Now generally available, dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Builders get one standard interface with built-in permission and DLP checks, and native human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmations for sensitive actions. They also reject non-agent OAuth clients and work with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s prompt-injection screening service. Workspace CLI : Now generally available for local agents, terminal workflows, and automation, providing structured JSON outputs and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services. Google Cloud Agent Gateway : A protocol-native gateway for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) traffic on Google Cloud. It verifies Agent Identities against Agent Registry, enforces IAM policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor. Together, these interfaces give AI agents open, protocol-native paths built on standards like MCP and A2A. Permissions, confirmations, prompt screening, and audit logging happen automatically, while traditional apps continue to run on existing REST APIs. Consistent controls across every agent workflow Those interfaces sit on a unified security model across Workspace and Google Cloud, with core controls shipping today: Policy checks on every request: Under our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum , AI agents must use Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI rather than existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027, giving builders time to transition. Every call is checked against your organization’s Workspace permissions, DLP rules, and classification labels. On Google Cloud, Agent Gateway enforces IAM and default-deny outbound rules at the protocol layer and routes custom checks through Service Extensions to Identity-Aware Proxy, your own policy engine, or third-party security tools. Separate agent identities and limits: Admins and users need to tell an AI agent apart from a traditional app or a person, and cap what it can do. Agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs , paired with least-privilege scopes, time-limited approvals (coming soon), and usage quotas (billing begins on April 1, 2027). On Google Cloud, agents receive their own Agent Identity in Agent Registry with no shared or long-lived keys, bounded by IAM policies and organization, folder, and project quotas. Those identities can also carry user-delegated authorization into Workspace when accessing mail or files. People stay in charge of high-impact actions: Routine work like creating drafts or summarizing documents runs autonomously, while critical changes require a person to sign off. In Workspace, MCP servers and the CLI enforce explicit user confirmation before agents send email, change Drive sharing permissions, or make bulk edits. On Google Cloud, policy can require multi-factor authentication or human approval before reading sensitive Cloud Storage buckets, changing IAM permissions, or modifying production infrastructure. Clear visibility and revocation: A one-time consent screen is not enough when agents run continuously. Workspace administrators can view, audit, and revoke AI agents in the admin console , and users will soon be able to view agent activity and revoke access to their emails and files. On Google Cloud, Security Command Center, Agent Observability, Cloud Audit Logs, and Wiz surface unusual behavior. Revoking a Cloud Agent Identity or OAuth grant stops access immediately. Boundaries for your most sensitive data: Coming soon in Workspace, AI access restrictions extend Workspace DLP and client-side encryption protections to agents. This will allow admins and users to block agents from accessing messages in Gmail and specific files and folders in Drive. On Google Cloud, VPC Service Controls, Principal Access Boundaries, and Context-Aware Access keep sensitive data inside designated perimeters and verified devices. Strict rules on your data afterward: Our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum sets clear boundaries for AI tools using Workspace APIs. It does not allow permanent raw storage, model training, extended retention of derived data, or API scraping. Derived and user data are removed within a defined window and when a user disconnects. On Google Cloud, Sensitive Data Protection masks sensitive fields before data leaves, and customer-managed or external encryption keys let you cut off access to Cloud agent memory stores immediately. Getting started Workspace developers: Start building with the Workspace MCP and CLI configuration guide , implement user confirmations via MCP and prompt-injection protection such as Model Armor, and review the Workspace AI Tools Addendum . Workspace administrators: Review connected apps and agents, configure DLP policies for your users, and monitor OAuth activity logs in the admin console . Google Cloud customers: Register Agent Identities in Agent Registry, place Agent Gateway and Model Armor in front of agents and MCP servers, configure MFA or human approval for sensitive actions, and review IAM, VPC Service Controls, and quota limits. With Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI generally available alongside Google Cloud’s agent protections, developers have an open, modern platform to build on. Organizations get the visibility and control to scale AI agents with confidence.

title: Enabling zero trust: ALLEN’s move to Chrome Enterprise Premium
raw_text: Editor’s note: Founded in 1988 in Kota, Rajasthan, ALLEN is one of India’s leading coaching institutions, serving over 400,000 students across 350+ classroom campuses in 78 cities. Here, the IT and Cybersecurity Leadership Team shares how they standardized on Chrome Enterprise Premium to secure sensitive data and enable zero trust across over 5,000 users. With a workforce that lives in the browser across a SaaS and multi-cloud estate, securing our digital environment is paramount. Our 5,000+ users include faculty, operations, engineering, contractors, and a large Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) population. Operating at this scale, our top priority is protecting student personally identifiable information (PII) flowing through web applications. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA), protecting this data is critical to regulatory compliance and maintaining brand trust. We needed security within the browser. The challenge of a fragmented browser estate We previously operated a mixed-browser environment, but managing multiple browsers made consistent policy enforcement and visibility challenging. We explored several options to standardize; however, our team didn’t want users to have to learn a new tool, and many of the options had high overhead costs. Testing and rolling out Chrome Enterprise Premium We implemented a phased Chrome Enterprise Premium pilot over a few weeks. Our team first validated the management capabilities in the Google Admin console by testing policy, deployment, extension controls, and reporting. Once we felt confident that Chrome Enterprise Premium provided our desired level of visibility, we rolled it out to several hundred users across various environments, including BYOD, Windows, and macOS. We deployed Safe Browsing and URL filtering for immediate threat protection, DLP rules to restrict copy/paste, downloads, and uploads on sensitive SaaS apps, and context-aware access to restrict application entry based on device posture. The proof of concept succeeded across all criteria including consistent policy enforcement, measurable reduction in risky-site and risky-download events, minimal user friction, and a centralized dashboard to give our teams visibility into managed user activity. The real decision moment came when we realized we could achieve a true Zero Trust posture. With Chrome Enterprise Premium as our backbone, access decisions now happen dynamically based on identity, device posture, and context. A teacher on a school-managed laptop enjoys seamless, full access. On a personal phone, that same educator can review materials without compromising security—downloads and clipboard sharing remain locked down. It delivers airtight data protection without disrupting daily instruction. A simpler, stronger foundation With Chrome Enterprise Premium, we replaced virtual desktops (VDIs) and fragmented security tools with built-in browser protection. Securing the browser itself means we no longer need to install heavy security software on every computer. This makes it easy to apply security policies to personal devices used by contractors and employees. Whether our team uses Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, iOS, or Android, we manage updates, policies, and audit reports from a single Google Admin console. Smart access controls Chrome Enterprise Premium ensures we only grant access when it is safe. Every time someone tries to log in, we verify three things: Identity: Is the user signed into their corporate account? Device: Is the laptop or phone managed and secure? Context: Where are they logging in from, and on what network? Stronger data protection We use Chrome Enterprise’s built-in features, such as Safe Browsing sandboxing and site isolation, and auto-updates to keep end users secure while they work on the web. These benefits plus Chrome Enterprise Premium prove that security does not have to slow down business. Employees work without security interruptions, and our IT team gets a single, clear audit trail across all devices. This helps us maintain high efficiency and supports our regulatory compliance efforts. Read more customer stories including how Mercari drove a 50% plus cost reduction with Chrome Enterprise Premium.

title: Data + AI Anywhere: AlloyDB Omni integration with local models
raw_text:
Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data? AlloyDB Omni , Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere. Built-in AI for your local environment AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment. Connecting to Gemma 4, Qwen3.8, and other local models You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8 . No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same. AlloyDB Omni calls a local model server directly from SQL — keeping prompts, data, and responses inside your environment. This setup enables entirely new use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance. Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet. Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time. Query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT customer_name,
 ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment,
 model_id => 'gemma4_llm') AS summary
FROM customer_feedback;

 Alice | The customer demands a refund for a double charge or they will cancel
 Bob | The user likes the product but requests dark mode support."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f0d2a6efc90>)])]> Next, you’ll see how to run queries like this yourself, step by step. Step 0: Before you begin In this example, we will use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to host the AlloyDB Omni database and local model. GKE gives us a standardized, reproducible environment but you can use the same setup on-prem or almost anywhere. We will assume you have already setup: A GKE cluster , and Kubernetes tools kubectl and Helm Step 1: Deploy the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes Operator We will use the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator to set up our AlloyDB Omni database. title: How Sinch modernized its enterprise data warehouse from Snowflake to BigQuery to power AI
raw_text: As the scale of global communications grows larger and larger, enterprise platforms must process billions of interactions with customers across a complex network of touchpoints without breaking them. A prime example is Sinch , one of the world’s leading cloud communications and customer engagement (CPaaS) companies, which processes billions of customer interactions, SMS routing events, voice calls, and transactional messages. Managing massive international messaging traffic brings significant architectural challenges, so Sinch built a distributed, multi-cloud data footprint across AWS and GCP, with separate Snowflake instances running in the EU, US, and Australia. To eliminate data silos, curb monthly billing spikes, establish a single governed source of truth, and unlock the next generation of predictive AI capabilities, Sinch partnered with Google Cloud Professional Services to migrate its enterprise data warehouse to Google BigQuery . Here’s how we engineered Sinch’s new, modern, cost-efficient, and AI-ready platform architecture The challenge: untangling distributed warehouses and escalating spikes Before it embarked on this modernization journey, Sinch faced several architectural and operational friction points: Cross-regional data sprawl: The company’s separate Snowflake instances in the EU, US, and Australia required intricate inter-region replication, which caused multi-directional dependencies and complex cross-warehouse data management. Resource spikes and commercial inefficiencies: Heavy monthly billing runs drove severe compute spikes in the US, even as other regions had underutilized capacity. High-volume scanning vs. dialect disparities: A single US email event table could generate up to 100 TB of daily scans. Meanwhile, mission-critical SQL relied on Snowflake-specific concurrency and table-swapping paradigms for concurrency validation, which lacked 1:1 equivalents in cloud-native SQL. “Google Cloud's engineering expertise helped us overcome several technical challenges during our migration, particularly around optimising Spark partitioning and restructuring incremental data loads. This allowed us to identify more efficient approaches, improve performance and ensure we built a scalable, reliable solution for the future.” Dan Peters, senior manager, Data Delivery, Sinch Phase 1: validating architecture with a target MVP To mitigate operational risk and prevent downtime for Sinch’s critical enterprise workloads (including ERP and NetSuite integrations), we initiated a phased migration framework: A use case pilot validation: The migration kicked off with a dedicated use case MVP that spanned 20 tables and 125 GB of refined data and automatically validated end-to-end data fidelity. Layered strategy for coupled pipelines: Rather than attempting to cleanly slice interconnected business domains in the EU, the team adopted a layered approach — migrating raw and base (bronze and silver) layers, establishing automated data ingestion, and stabilizing core entities before repointing consumption marts. Orchestration consolidation: Sinch consolidated 36 independent ETL workflows into a single parameterized orchestrator by using Google Cloud Workflows , which streamlined CI/CD deployment logic, and reduced operational overhead. Re-engineering for scale: key architectural pillars 1. Decoupled storage and optimized ingestion Sinch transitioned its data ingestion pipelines to Dataproc Serverless (running Apache Spark 3.5), which directly pulled refined data into native BigQuery tables from S3 and Databricks Unity Catalog. And to overcome batch quota limits and resource exhaustion on billion-row datasets, Sinch optimized jobs by increasing Spark repartitioning factors to 50. For its incremental pipelines, the team eliminated data duplication while minimizing query read costs by replacing slow, keyless merge statements with an optimized insert-and-overwrite windowing strategy. 2. AI-assisted SQL and macro translation In order to accelerate the translation of more than 1,200 dbt models across global projects, Sinch utilized Google Cloud BigQuery Migration Service alongside a set of custom AI translation skills. Here’s how: The team refactored Snowflake-specific table versioning and concurrency management paradigms into deterministic transaction blocks and view abstraction pointers. This ensured atomic updates and consistent data access. Sinch leveraged specialized Google skills for other regional migration — specifically the dbt-sf-to-bq-translator skill powered by the underlying BigQuery Translation API — to automate the conversion of dbt models from Snowflake to BigQuery SQL syntax. This significantly reduced manual refactoring effort and error rates. Concurrency checks that relied on row-level locking were redesigned into serialized batch validations. Integer overflow risks in massive calculation tables were solved by adopting a tiered precision strategy (favoring NUMERIC over BIGNUMERIC ), which cut storage costs and preserved absolute precision. “Migrating over a thousand complex dbt models and translating legacy SQL required a robust, automated approach. Google Cloud's guidance on query restructuring helped us streamline pipeline development and remove compilation blockers. The team shared best practices for migrating code from Snowflake to BigQuery, such as replacing Snowflake SWAP WITH and hybrid-table patterns with BigQuery time travel. They also helped us build workflows that copy data from Snowflake to BigQuery and run our dbt jobs along the way, which sped up our move to BigQuery.” Varun Gupta, Senior Data Engineer, Sinch Real-world business impact By completing the migration, Sinch successfully transformed the operational bottleneck of its global data footprint into a driver of enterprise growth: Metric / capability Before (Snowflake) After (BigQuery) Pipeline performance High data churn; lengthy multi-hour batch runs Significantly faster query and pipeline processing speeds across billions of records Compute and billing efficiency Unpredictable month-end billing spikes Predictable capacity management with BigQuery reservations and slot autoscaling AI readiness Segmented data warehouses requiring external pipelines Native BQML and Vertex AI decision intelligence platform Looking ahead With its core European warehouse workloads stabilized on BigQuery and data validation consistently outperforming legacy benchmarks, Sinch is now expanding this modern blueprint across its Australian (SMB) and US analytics. The SMB instance migration is already in progress and is utilizing Antigravity skills for the Snowflake to BigQuery translation. By unifying data storage, operational governance, and serverless compute, Sinch has built a resilient platform that delivers real-time messaging reliability today while positioning the company to capture the full potential of enterprise AI tomorrow.

title: Attackers exploited an Azure API Management flaw to steal secrets, Microsoft warns
raw_text: Microsoft is warning customers that attackers exploited a flaw in Azure API Management Classic tiers to steal stored secrets, an intrusion that Norway’s National Security Authority has linked to breaches at two energy companies and says organizations should assume exposed credentials were compromised. Microsoft said in an Azure Service Health security advisory sent to customers that it identified the vulnerability on Nov. 18 and deployed a mitigation the following day. The advisory, tracking ID MZK9-GH0, said the exposure began before Microsoft found the flaw, reported Bleeping Computer. The company said in the advisory that “an unauthorized party could have used the issue to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances.” The potentially exposed information includes secrets stored in Named Values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs, the report added. Microsoft warned that its mitigation does not invalidate previously compromised credentials and that affected customers must rotate potentially exposed secrets and investigate suspicious activity. The advisory said only the Classic tiers of the service are affected, not Azure API Management v2, the report added. The potential exposure was not limited to a theoretical security risk. Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) subsequently linked cyberattacks against two energy companies to the vulnerability, providing evidence of exploitation in an operational environment. Norway tells customers to assume exposure In a security advisory published November 20 and updated November 23, NSM said an unidentified actor had actively targeted access tokens, secrets, and Named Values stored in Azure API Management. “Earlier this week, NSM became aware of a vulnerability in Azure API Management (APIM) that affects several Norwegian businesses,” NSM said in the advisory, translated from Norwegian. It said the vulnerability should now be closed, but asked organizations to take measures anyway. “Anyone with Azure API Manager must assume that their secrets and named values ​​are out of whack,” the advisory added. “This means that the business must roll back all tokens and secrets.” In the advisory, NSM’s director of operational cybersecurity, Martin Albert-Hoff, said the vulnerability was first discovered by Norway’s energy sector. The agency identified Equinor and Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations and said the vulnerability had also affected organizations in other countries and sectors. Equinor disclosed a cyberattack against some of its IT systems on November 17. In an update published November 20 , the company said the attack had been stopped, production was running normally, and there was no indication that data had been stolen or altered. A day later, Skagerak Energi reported an attempted cyberattack against some of its IT systems. The company said the incident had not affected its operations or production and that there was no indication that information had been compromised. NSM warned that public disclosure of the vulnerability could encourage additional threat actors to attempt exploitation. “When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors may attempt to exploit it,” the agency said in its advisory (translated from Norwegian), adding that the rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence was affecting the threat environment. Neither Microsoft’s advisory nor NSM’s notice includes a CVE identifier for the flaw. Urgent need to rotate credentials Microsoft’s mitigation closed the unauthorized management-plane access path, but it advised customers to investigate whether their APIM instances were accessed before the fix and whether stored credentials could have been exposed, the report added. In a November 21 post on its Azure Integration Services blog , Microsoft published guidance on identifying and rotating credentials configured in Azure API Management. The guidance covers subscription keys, Named Values containing secrets, backend credentials, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect client secrets, connection strings, and credentials written directly into API policies. Microsoft recommended that organizations rotate credentials at the systems where they were originally issued, rather than simply updating their values in APIM. “Updating the value in API Management alone does not invalidate the old credential,” the company said in the blog post, as per the report. NSM has issued more extensive recommendations, advising organizations using Azure API Management to assume that their secrets and Named Values may have been exposed and to rotate all associated tokens and secrets. The agency also published a patch check. According to NSM, instances on the 0.52.x branch are patched from build 31936, and those on 0.53.x are from build 31938. V2 and Consumption tier instances are not vulnerable, the agency said. Organizations with unpatched instances should contact Microsoft directly, and those that see signs of compromise should contact NSM, the advisory said. Cloud security researcher Anders Kristiansen, who published detection and hunting guidance after the advisories, said patching alone is not enough. “If you run APIM, patching isn’t the end of it,” Kristiansen wrote in a blog post. His rotation list includes backend credentials, app registration secrets, subscription keys, the Key Vault secrets the service references, and tenant access keys. Microsoft did not immediately respond to CSO’s request for comment.

title: CrowdStrike buys missing network security piece in $43.9B Zscaler deal
raw_text: CrowdStrike agreed to acquire cloud security company Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal on Monday, combining endpoint protection with zero-trust network security in one of the largest cybersecurity acquisitions ever and intensifying the industry’s race to build broad security platforms. The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform, which focuses on endpoint, identity and cloud security, with Zscaler’s cloud-delivered network security and zero-trust access capabilities. CrowdStrike said the combined company is expected to begin with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The acquisition also addresses a strategic gap in CrowdStrike’s portfolio. While the company has expanded beyond endpoint protection into identity, cloud security and threat intelligence, Zscaler brings an established security service edge (SSE) and zero-trust network access platform. “With Zscaler, CrowdStrike will enter network security, cybersecurity’s largest single addressable market segment,” CrowdStrike said in a statement. The companies expect the deal to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal 2028, subject to approval by Zscaler shareholders and regulators, the statement added. The deal is larger than Google’s $32 billion purchase of Wiz and Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk , both completed earlier this year. From partnership to one platform CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz framed the deal around AI in the statement. “With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely,” Kurtz said. Yih Khai Wong, research director at IDC, said the deal fits a pattern of larger security vendors “buying into adjacent control points rather than building them organically.” Until now, he said, CrowdStrike “lacks a strong, owned network/SSE layer.” The two companies are not starting from scratch. The statement described the relationship as one of CrowdStrike’s largest technology alliances, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 integrations. CrowdStrike argued that a partnership integrates separate products, while one company integrates “the data, the roadmap, the go-to-market, and the commercial model.” Wong said the existing partnership already delivers much of the correlation value. Ownership adds “control over the roadmap and the pace of integration,” he said. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said the merger buys “fluency rather than new vocabulary.” One owner means a single data model and faster correlation, he said, but that gain is “narrower than any merger pitch will claim.” He advised CISOs to ask the vendors to show, in their own environments, which outcomes today’s integration cannot already reach. One contract, one renewal The commercial plan is central to the deal. After closing, customers of either company will be able to buy the other’s products on a single Falcon Flex contract, the statement said. CrowdStrike identified about 8,000 Zscaler customers that do not yet use CrowdStrike, and said it expects about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing. “Falcon Flex will bring Zscaler onto the commercial model customers already use, so they commit once and expand from there,” the statement said. Gogia said that model shifts leverage over time. “Consolidation is sold at the first signature and priced at the second,” he said. The second signature comes at renewal, he said, when the supplier holds more of the estate and the buyer holds fewer alternatives. He advised CFOs and CISOs to price consolidation offers at their first full renewal, and to keep one credible alternative alive in each layer they consolidate. Wong said consolidation “addresses real integration challenges for enterprises that commit to a single platform, while quietly reducing the leverage and flexibility of those that don’t.” Enterprises in heavily regulated industries that need best-of-breed tools may find bundled platforms fall short, he added. Two layers, one release train CrowdStrike also expects $500 million in annualized cost synergies within 18 to 24 months of closing, mainly from optimizing data center infrastructure, vendors and operations, the statement said. For security teams, the question is whether that consolidation reaches the products themselves. Today the Falcon sensor and Zscaler’s client run as separate agents on separate clouds, with separate release schedules, Gogia said. “A merged agent, a shared update pipeline, or a single control plane would change that,” Gogia said. “One bad release would then reach the device and the way in together.” Wong said CISOs should build that scenario into their business continuity plans, since “an incident could affect both the endpoint agent and the access control plane.” Gogia advised teams to map every access rule that depends on CrowdStrike’s device posture check, and to keep a fallback route that relies on neither vendor. Customers that pair Zscaler with another endpoint product, or Falcon with another SSE provider, should get integration commitments in writing, he said. “Neutrality promised in a blog post lasts exactly as long as the blog post.” Until the deal closes, both companies will continue to operate independently, the statement added.

The deal brings together CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform, which focuses on endpoint, identity and cloud security, with Zscaler’s cloud-delivered network security and zero-trust access capabilities. CrowdStrike said the combined company is expected to begin with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The acquisition also addresses a strategic gap in CrowdStrike’s portfolio.

title: Clever AI prompt ideas every security leader should steal
raw_text: For all the talk of AI use by attackers and defenders, little attention is paid to ways CISOs and their security pros can leverage AI uniquely to expediate tasks, cut through the noise, facilitate decision-making, and potentially save big on auditing. Several specific AI prompts can help security leaders and staff handle multiple critical tasks not typically associated with AI for cyber defense, such as risk management, compliance, policy development, and critical thinking. Developing truly useful prompts isn’t particularly easy, however, because it often requires a significant amount of research and effort, not to mention lots of fine-tuning, which can take security teams away from other critical tasks. Fortunately, the security community is here to help, with advice on unique prompt ideas that have greatly aided them in strengthening security, facilitating decision-making, and saving time for hands-on defense. Create an adversarial assistant to control damage — and cut down AI slop Dzmitry Romanovadvocates establishing an AI prompt that acts as a second security reviewer to help catch latent problems before any damage occurs. The key, though, is to give it an adversarial twist so that it looks at a situation from the attacker’s perspective while critiquing the human security reviewer’s ideas. “What am I missing? What attack vectors or edge cases should I inspect?” is the kind of questions Romanov, cybersecurity team lead and senior security engineer at the Belarusian State University of Informatics and Radioelectronics and cybersecurity team lead with Vention, an AI-enabled software development company, such a prompt can help with. “This approach works most effectively when analyzing architecture or code, while reviewing penetration test results, and auditing cloud configurations, as well as when modeling threats and assessing risks,” Romanov says. Philippe Dourassov, AI pentest lead at Aikido Security, offers another version of the adversarial agent prompt — in this case against agent helpers. When agents are used to generate security reports, engineers often find themselves buried under irrelevant findings — noise, says Dourassov. However, when a second agent is deployed to analyze the quality of another agent’s work, and correct its output, the result can be surprisingly efficient. “The first agent has been given a task and will do everything it can to convince the humans that its results are relevant and critical, as this is what the agent would consider a good job,” Dourassov says, noting that his adversarial agent is basically a reviewer. “Its task is to eliminate noise, rectify claims, and highlight the true importance of the first agent’s result.” The agent’s definition of a good job, Dourassov says, is being able to eliminate noise and supply only signal to the human user. “Therefore, it’s essential to use an adversarial prompt to review agents’ output, so we ensure we don’t face security fatigue from AI slop.” Take care of business Brandyn Fisher, senior penetration testing technical lead at business and technology consulting firm Centric Consulting, offers three prompt ideas that CISOs can deploy on a regular basis to aid with their work. The first Fisher uses is a vendor due diligence prompt. “I feed it our organization’s risk thresholds and the vendor in question, and it benchmarks that vendor, sweeps the Internet for security pages, breach history, customer reviews, complaints, and recent news, then returns a structured report I can review and validate quickly,” he explains. Fisher also recommends crafting a professional writing prompt that takes technical analysis and reframes it into language a CIO or board will actually engage with. Gen AI pioneer Kevin Surace offered a similar prompt idea to attendees of this year’s CSO Conference and Awards in May. “Translate the SOC for the boardroom. This is important. They don’t really understand what’s going on,” Surace said. “The prompt here: ‘You are writing the cyber risk section of the board deck. You have four minutes of board time. Below is ninety days of security operations data. Produce three slides for a board that does not know what lateral movement means.’ This is so useful.” Fisher’s third prompt for CISOs is a tech debt reduction prompt “where I list our technology stack and have AI flag underutilized tools, overlapping capabilities, and consolidation opportunities,” he says. Fisher advises building each of his recommendations as a standing agent, project, or skill, or whatever your AI platform supports, so you have a static, repeatable spot to run it instead of rewriting the prompt from scratch every time. Don’t wait for a perfect first version, Fisher adds. “Get an initial prompt working, even if it’s rough, and have AI help draft the instructions themselves.” Expect to revise it several times before it’s reliable. Challenge your policies and content At the CSO Conference, Surace also highlighted how CISOs can use AI prompts to audit their policy libraries. “You are a compliance auditor. I am giving you our policy library and the current text of NIST CSF 2.0, ISO 27001:2022 Annex A, SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05, and the EU AI Act. Produce three lists,” his example prompt began, directing the LLM to find contradictions, gaps, and stale language — the kind of analysis big firms do for six figures in 12 weeks, he noted. Olivia Brännlund, CISO at Outpost24, a cybersecurity and risk management firm, regularly uses a similar prompt that turns AI into an internal auditor and security advisor. The tool reviews policy, processes, risk assessment, incident reports, contract clauses, and specific customer requirements. Brännlund believes that organizations that treat AI as an expert reviewer typically obtain more value than organizations that treat it as a content generator. The key, she states, “isn’t using AI to write content, but using it to challenge content.” Tying together policy review and the adversarial assistant concept, Surace advised CSO conference attendees to also “red team your own runbook.” “You are the operations lead for Scattered Spider. I am giving you our incident response playbook, our detection coverage matrix, and our on-call tree. Identify the five places this runbook fails,” his prompt started, probing for wrong assumptions, bottlenecks, escalation path weaknesses, and so on. “It’s totally worth doing this,” he said. “You will have more information in an hour than you, than you’ve ever had. Vet your agent’s capabilities and weaknesses Chris Hughes advises asking your model what your AI agents can actually do. “Give it an agent’s configuration, tool manifest, or MCP server definitions and ask it to summarize the agent’s effective permissions, the blast radius if it’s compromised, and whether a human approval step exists anywhere in the workflow,” says Hughes, who teaches in the CISO and Leading Enterprise Agentic AI Development Certificate Program at Carnegie Mellon University’s Heinz College. “Most organizations are deploying agents faster than they’re documenting what those agents can reach, and this closes the gap in minutes.” The model turns work that normally requires a senior architect into something an analyst can run at design review, before deployment, and after every change. It also surfaces assumptions the team stopped questioning, Hughes says. The model doesn’t share your blind spots, so it tends to flag the over-permissioned tool or the missing approval gate that everyone walked past, he notes. Once tuned, the prompt becomes a control in its own right rather than a one-off exercise. Embrace deep inspection Steve Tait, CTO at cloud security firm Skyhigh Security, suggests tailoring an AI prompt to take aim at AI prompts themselves, noting that perhaps the most important capability is a prompt response inspection that understands both data and intent. “CISOs should be able to determine not only whether sensitive information is entering or leaving an AI service, but whether a user or agent is attempting something risky—such as prompt injection, jailbreaks, policy evasion, credential exposure or unauthorized data access,” he says, adding that as AI agents become more common, that same inspection and policy model needs to extend beyond human prompts to agent-driven interactions. Tait believes that CISOs should think of prompt security as a platform control that needs to work across every major access path to AI, including Secure Web Gateway (SWG), zero trust network access, browser-based access, and APIs. “The goal should not be to plug a single gap for one AI application, but to establish a consistent policy and inspection layer wherever users or agents interact with AI services,” he explains. “This also means choosing an approach that can support hybrid environments, including organizations that still rely heavily on on-premises SWG infrastructure.”
summary: For all the talk of AI use by attackers and defenders, little attention is paid to ways CISOs and their security pros can leverage AI uniquely to expediate tasks, cut through the noise, facilitate decision-making, and potentially save big on auditing. Several specific AI prompts can help security leaders and staff handle multiple critical tasks not typically associated with AI for cyber defense, such as risk management, compliance, policy development, and critical thinking. Developing truly useful prompts isn’t particularly easy, however, because it often requires a significant amount of research and effort, not to mention lots of fine-tuning, which can take security teams away from other critical tasks. Fortunately, the security community is here to help, with advice on unique prompt ideas that have greatly aided them in strengthening security, facilitating decision-making, and saving time for hands-on defense.

title: Amazon CTO Werner Vogels: Computing to converge with biology
raw_text:
Technology must decode how biology handles information, because nature handles vast amounts of data with a fraction of the energy used in datacentres.

Meanwhile, security and sovereignty need to be built into systems and software at their inception, and scientists will find new cures for diseases that were unattainable before artificial intelligence (AI).

And to top all of this, new ways for humans to interface with information systems will lead to IT that can read our minds.

Those are the short versions of Amazon chief technology officer Werner Vogels’ predictions for 2027. He unveiled them this week, and started with a word he said now outranks “AI” as the term of the moment. That word is “human”.

“Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year is ‘human’ – it’s not ‘AI’, it’s not ‘artificial’, it’s ‘human’,” said Vogels.

He described himself as “a technology optimist”, but also “a realist”. “I believe we build technology not for technology’s sake, but to support humans, to make our lives better,” he said.

Vogels has spent 22 years as Amazon’s chief technology officer. His 2026 predictions, published this time last year, included the dawn of the renaissance developer – developers who blend creativity and technical expertise, like Leonardo da Vinci.

1. Computing should take its lead from biology

Vogels’ first prediction is that computing will “return to biology” to learn how to use far fewer resources. The trigger, he said, is the enormous resource usage of today’s AI models, which need “millions of central processing units [CPUs] and graphics processing units [GPUs] – massive data storage”. The human brain does the same job far more cheaply. “Our brain, even with the 86 billion neurons in it, only uses 20 watts,” said Vogels.

On a 2023 trip to Melbourne, he visited Cortical Labs, where human neurons grown on silicon learned tasks by trial and error. Its first installations came online this summer, each built on the CL1, “a self-contained computer that keeps living human neurons alive on a silicon chip”. A CL1 holds about 200,000 neurons and runs on 25 to 30 watts.

“A full rack of 30 draws under 1,000 watts, while a rack of high-end GPUs requires more than 600 kilowatts,” said Vogels.

Brain-inspired chips at the University of Texas at Dallas learn by strengthening connections when neurons on either side fire together – “Hebbian learning” – which suits edge computing, where “a little chip that sits in the tyre of your car” keeps learning how you drive.

“The next major breakthrough in computing will come from understanding how biology does more with less,” he said.

Asked how society should weigh AI’s cost, Vogels said resource use matters most. “Even the smallest LLMs [large language models] take enormous amounts of energy to just train, and inference is not free,” he said. “The more we can reduce the resource usage and the cheaper we can make this, the more we have an opportunity to make all of this technology available for everyone, not just for the largest, biggest companies.” That, Vogels added, “has a democratisation effect”.

2. Every system will defend itself

His second prediction is about security, and he frames it as already happening. “In 2027, adversarial testing will move into every phase of software development,” said Vogels. “When WannaCry spread through systems around the world in 2017, it ran on an exploit stolen from the NSA and struck 59 days after a patch was available.”

That head start has gone, he said. “Agents now bring expertise with them, run in swarms, and are becoming so cheap that the cost of running hundreds of them in parallel is negligible for an attacker,” explained Vogels.

In April, Anthropic pointed “1,000 copies of Claude” at OpenBSD. Across 1,000 runs, the work cost less than $20,000, he said, and found a 27-year-old flaw in its TCP stack that could crash any host. The individual run that found it cost less than $50.

The answer, he said, is to run the same techniques in reverse before software ships. “Just like with Toyota’s Andon cord, which allows any employee to stop the line when a defect is found, they will prevent any known defect from shipping,” said Vogels.

Amazon already runs Autonomous Threat Analysis, where one group of tens of thousands of agents invents attacks and another tests whether defences catch them. “It’s still the humans that make decisions,” he said. “We will trust systems because the people who built them attacked them first.”

3. Sovereignty to become a non-functional requirement

Vogels’ third prediction is that sovereignty will move from an after-the-fact audit to a requirement designed in from the start, the way cost is handled in his Frugal Architect framework. Of its “seven laws”, the first says, “Cost becomes a non-functional requirement”. Sovereignty, he argues, should follow the same logic.

That means deciding encryption, key management and location up front, but also being able to change things. “Systems now change faster than any audit can follow,” he said. “An AI agent can add a replica in another region or swap a model in minutes.”

It comes down to risk analysis, said Vogels. “Organisations that wall off every workload in the most restrictive environment they can find and apply the same rules to a lunch menu as to a patient record will pay in cost, in resilience, and in access to new capabilities,” he said.

Frugality, added Vogels, was always about spending deliberately, because “isolation is not the same thing as control”.

Asked how sovereignty should be built in, he said teams must decide up front what restrictions apply to each class of data, and that the answer runs wider than where datacentres sit. “It’s not just about the location where the datacentres are,” said Vogels. “It is also about what services are available, what services do you rely on? Who do you trust?”

4. Scientists and agents will find new cures

Vogels’ fourth prediction is that researchers working with AI agents will find new treatments. Before becoming a technologist, he worked in cancer research. Vogels argued that treating disease as a single entity misses how differently it affects each person. “When we think about disease, we think about disease as an entity, but it’s not,” he said.

“Before this decade is out, scientists working with agents will discover a cure for a disease that today’s medicine can only manage,” added Vogels.

In August, in a late-stage melanoma trial, a personalised messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) cancer vaccine used with pembrolizumab cut the risk of recurrence and distant metastasis compared with using pembrolizumab alone, with machine learning selecting the vaccine’s targets from each patient’s tumour.

Agents handle the brute-force search, said Vogels. “It’s not just looking for a needle in a haystack, it is 1,000 haystacks and there’s still only one needle,” he said. “It’s like having a door that’s locked, and you have a billion keys and you need to figure out which key will open this particular door. That’s just brute force work, and agents can help scientists with that brute force work.”

5. The mind will become readable

Vogels saved his favourite prediction for last. Namely, “the mind becomes readable”.

He called the brain “the most amazing machine in existence”, which we have forced to talk to the world through a keyboard, a mouse and touch. Implants already restore hearing and sight, but few healthy people want surgery.

“A 2024 YouGov survey found only one in five would consider a brain implant, and in the United States, that fell to 11%,” he said.

But the non-invasive route is advancing, added Vogels. This summer, researchers at Meta and several European labs used a magnetoencephalography scanner outside the skull to record the magnetic signals the brain produced as people typed.

“It reached 61% word accuracy on 90 hours of recordings, and kept improving as more data came in,” he said, citing a 50% improvement in some stroke therapies.

The money is following, added Vogels. In six months, Chinese companies in the field raised more than 4.6 billion yuan, while the UK is putting £69m into new neural interfaces.

What excites him, he said, is not command and control, but amplification. “Interfaces that let you catch an innovative idea at the edge of your mind before it’s gone,” said Vogels. “Instead of having to rely on a chatbot, maybe we should just supersize our brains with this technology. The most successful technologies we can build will be those that amplify our unique human skills.”

title: Third-party support: Risks and opportunities
raw_text:
Analyst Forrester has reported that with the ongoing global economic uncertainty, some organisations are avoiding allocating funds for large applications and business transformation efforts.

In its Third-party software support offers a low-cost alternative report, Forrester says those organisations with budgetary concerns are tightening IT spending for on-premise applications, and reserving funds for mandatory application upgrades and modernisations only. 

Due to inflation, Forrester notes that many software providers are increasing their annual maintenance and support fees for existing customers.

“Sometimes these increases occur every year, leading to a significant cumulative increase over time,” Forrester notes in the report.

There is also the use of the so-called “carrot or stick” technique, which Forrester says is often used by software providers to motivate their on-premise customers to move to a software as a service (SaaS) or hosted cloud offering.

Forrester’s research shows that in the enterprise software market, the global move to the cloud is steady, but it’s not as rapid as for non-enterprise software.

This, according to Forrester, puts an additional burden on software providers to maintain technical, functional, product and security personnel to support older software versions. “For customers that don’t have price protection language in their contracts or see no way to avoid the certainty of cost increases, moving to TPSS [third-party support service] is a viable alternative with comprehensive SLAs [service-level agreements],” the analyst states.

Read more about third party software support

  • Does third-party support make sense: We speak to a Rimini Street customer about their experience of managing an Oracle ERP.
  • How Specsavers saved on Oracle costs: The high street opticians chain has swapped Oracle support for Spinnaker third-party support to help drive its business transformation.

Cost savings can be significant, especially as IT departments can keep a stable enterprise system running using third-party support, while they focus on areas of the business to generate additional value, such as a new artificial intelligence (AI) initiative.

Cyber risks

But CIOs will need to be prepared to answer questions on how safe an enterprise system protected by third-party support can be, especially with the advent of AI-powered cyber attacks. If a cyber security patch is released or an advisory published on the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures database, hackers are alerted there is a known weakness in an enterprise system.

AI has made it possible to craft an exploit extremely quickly, often before IT admins have fully patched the vulnerable systems. IT departments can only download patches from their enterprise software provider so long as they have an active support contract.

If support is provided by a third party, access to that patch is simply not available or not authorised. An IT department downloading patches it is officially no longer able to licence risks incurring a software piracy claim.

According to James Harvey, chief technology officer at Rimini Street for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, IT departments are thinking differently about their technology stack than they did decades ago, especially with the introduction of modern, cloud-native architectures, which influences how they consider the support of enterprise software.

“I think the concept of patching, as we’ve known it for the best part of 30 to 40 years, is changing,” he said. “As we see enterprises construct IT differently, using less fully packaged applications, and more containerised microservices with multiple landing zones, there is less of a system of record that may lose their data. Instead, they have a very wide federated data model across multiple applications.”

Since their customers no longer have access to the patches supplied by enterprise software providers, third-party support providers need to take a different approach to securing their customers’ IT systems. “We have an organisation internally that enables our customers to harden everything around their enterprise system,” said Harvey. “Rather than a patch that works from the technology up, we harden IT security from the business down.”

“You’re still getting the same protection, but in a different way,” he said. “It’s not less secure. It’s as good – if not better – and it’s as safe.”

title: Peer calls on prime minister to intervene in DWP subpostmaster prosecutions review
raw_text:
UK prime minister Andy Burnham is being urged to intervene and deliver the promised government review of subpostmaster prosecutions by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Peer Prem Sikka has written to Burnham asking him to personally end the “unacceptable” delay to a review that was first promised nearly two years ago.

Around 100 subpostmasters and branch staff were prosecuted by the DWP with support from the Post Office. Following the increased public awareness of the Post Office scandal, which included hundreds of wrongful subpostmaster convictions, the government said it would review the DWP prosecutions in February 2025.

Speaking on behalf of the government in the House of Lords at the time, peer Maggie Jones, in response to a question from fellow peer Prem Sikka, said: “My noble friend Lord Sikka raised a question about the DWP convictions. I can assure him that the minister for transformation is looking into this, a review is being established, and I hope to provide more information about that.”

In his letter to Burnham, Sikka wrote: “I am writing to urge you to intervene to ensure the government’s promises are delivered.”

He added: “My focus is on the 100 or so prosecutions of subpostmasters by the DWP, dating back to 1996. Despite an announcement of a review 21 months ago, nothing has happened.”

In August 2026, the government had not yet appointed a reviewer of the cases. According to a freedom of information response at the time, 113 people applied for the position, which will look at the prosecutions of subpostmasters by the DWP between 1996 and 2018.

A DWP spokesperson said: “We remain committed to an independent review of the department’s approach, and will update on the appointment of a reviewer in due course.”

The DWP said these were complex investigations backed by evidence including surveillance, stolen benefit books and handwriting analysis, and that decisions on convictions were for the courts, not DWP. It added that the review will assess the steps DWP took to gather and review information on Horizon-period prosecutions, and whether more could have been done to strengthen that work.

Focus turned on the DWP after the Post Office Horizon controversy hit the mainstream following an ITV drama about the scandal, which saw hundreds of subpostmasters wrongly prosecuted following account shortfalls.

These discrepancies were caused by errors in the Post Office Horizon system used in branches and affected thousands of subpostmasters. More than 900 subpostmaster convictions, which had been based on data from Horizon, were overturned en masse through an act of Parliament in May 2024.

The DWP worked with the Post Office on its subpostmaster prosecutions, and it has emerged that prosecutions of people using various systems at Post Office branches could also be flawed.

In January 2026, Neil Hudgell, lawyer at Hudgell Solicitors, told Computer Weekly that his law firm is pursuing its own investigations on behalf of clients and already had “a couple of cases lined up” to send to the CCRC.

“We’ve unearthed some interesting things that we think impact the safety of convictions, so we’re not waiting around on DWP themselves,” said Hudgell. “Someone needs to lean on the DWP, because it’s not good enough. [The longer it takes], the more suspicion subpostmasters have that there’s something to hide.”

UK prime minister Andy Burnham is being urged to intervene and deliver the promised government review of subpostmaster prosecutions by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).

Peer Prem Sikka has written to Burnham asking him to personally end the “unacceptable” delay to a review that was first promised nearly two years ago.

Around 100 subpostmasters and branch staff were prosecuted by the DWP with support from the Post Office. Following the increased public awareness of the Post Office scandal, which included hundreds of wrongful subpostmaster convictions, the government said it would review the DWP prosecutions in February 2025.

Speaking on behalf of the government in the House of Lords at the time, peer Maggie Jones, in response to a question from fellow peer Prem Sikka, said: “My noble friend Lord Sikka raised a question about the DWP convictions. I can assure him that the minister for transformation is looking into this, a review is being established, and I hope to provide more information about that.”

In his letter to Burnham, Sikka wrote: “I am writing to urge you to intervene to ensure the government’s promises are delivered.”

He added: “My focus is on the 100 or so prosecutions of subpostmasters by the DWP, dating back to 1996. Despite an announcement of a review 21 months ago, nothing has happened.”

In August 2026, the government had not yet appointed a reviewer of the cases. According to a freedom of information response at the time, 113 people applied for the position, which will look at the prosecutions of subpostmasters by the DWP between 1996 and 2018.

A DWP spokesperson said: “We remain committed to an independent review of the department’s approach, and will update on the appointment of a reviewer in due course.”

The DWP said these were complex investigations backed by evidence including surveillance, stolen benefit books and handwriting analysis, and that decisions on convictions were for the courts, not DWP.

title: UK cyber legislation fails to tackle real-world resilience
raw_text:
From mid-July through into October, more than a fair amount of my House of Lords colleagues' and my time has been filled with trying to improve the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill (CSRB). A milestone, of sorts, came when the bill passed its third reading on 2 November.

The bill will be considered in the House of Commons today (24 November) with over 100 amendments, 64 of which dropped from the government a day before we were due to begin our detailed consideration - sweet timing? Even with so many changes, the bill is significantly insufficient in so many critical areas.

Shaking up cyber law

For security leaders across the UK, the legislation represents the biggest shake-up to the Network and Information Systems (NIS) regulations since 2018.

Originally introduced in November 2025 and carried over between parliamentary sessions, the bill aims to close gaps that have widened as attackers target interconnected supply chains. It pulls managed service providers (MSPs), datacentres, large load-controllers, and designated critical suppliers into regulatory scope alongside essential operators in energy, water, transport, health, and digital infrastructure.

It also compresses incident reporting to an initial alert within 24 hours and a fuller report within 72, grants ministers powers to issue directions, allows regulators to recover costs, and raises maximum penalties up to £17m or 4% of global turnover.

All of this is very much known. What remains at best opaque is what the Commons will make of the amended bill and what happens when it begins its staggered roll-out, still with so many gaps.

Real-world resilience

There will be much ado about regulation through 2027 and 2028, but will this be enough and in time? To answer with brevity, at this stage, I offer just a few short words to contemplate - and they would be: impact on real-world resilience.

From my perspective, we were able to get two important changes through at report stage on 26 October. First, forcing a 12-month review of the NIS regime, and second, a register of state actors posing cyber threats to the UK. We must wait to see what ministers will make of this.

Even when royal assent finally arrives, professional practitioners in the security field point to a long list of gaps that the bill leaves unresolved. We tried.

Perhaps the most glaring omission is who finds themselves outside the imposed perimeter.

While expanding into MSPs and datacentres addresses a major weakness in the digital supply chain, the framework remains restricted to essential services and designated critical suppliers.

Outside the perimeter

As our House of Lords National Resilience Select Committee has recently rightly warned, major commercial enterprises find themselves outside that perimeter. Retail is currently out. Think about the terrible time we all shared during Covid. Retail is significant, some might even suggest critical - I would.

Similarly, last year’s Jaguar Land Rover cyber attack had a catastrophic impact that went throughout the motor industry supply chain, bleeding out into the wider economy and registering in a reduction to that quarter’s GDP. Is a cyber attack in the motor industry, impacting GDP, significant? Critical?

The 24-hour and 72-hour reporting requirements were, well, very much reported upon. But is there any necessarily helpful link between the rapidity of the reporting and that of the recovery? Colleagues and I at both committee and report stages of the legislation continued to make these points to little or no avail.

Read more about the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill

  • MPs propose ‘kill switch’ to shut down rogue AI systems - An amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill proposes giving the government a ‘kill switch’ to close datacentres hosting AI if they pose a critical threat to UK infrastructure or national security.
  • Are we mistaking regulation for resilience? We have a growing number of cyber compliance regulations, yet our country’s cyber resilience remains fragile. What is going wrong?
  • IT services companies and datacentres face regulation as cyber security bill reaches Parliament - The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill will require large IT services companies, including datacentres, to report security incidents within 24 hours.

Though the bill is clear on the clocks, it is less so when it comes to who is responsible for fixing underlying vulnerabilities or how remediation must be carried out.

We debated at length issues around board accountability, senior competence and more - all left out. There is nothing currently on the face of the bill in primary legislation - all is left, at best, to regulation.

And what of skills, training, development and recruitment in the first instance? Industry research has regularly highlighted widespread cyber skills shortages across UK organisations and public bodies, set alongside a surge in reported cyber incidents.

And spare a thought for the smaller firms in the supply chain facing a double squeeze - even if not regulated directly, they will feel pressure through stricter contracts and procurement rules.

We tried over several sessions to secure a dedicated national cyber support service for small and medium-sized businesses. Sensible – but not accepted.

Regulating emerging technologies

The bill also leaves structural questions hanging over enforcement and emerging tech.

Our efforts to stand up a single cyber security regulator to end cross-sector inconsistency were dashed by the government’s preference for a sectoral model, leaving organisations navigating different regulators in varying degrees of fog.

This allies clearly with calls I have made for years now on the need for a single, right-sized, horizontally focused AI regulator - so it should be with cyber and yet, in the UK as a consequence of this bill, it is not.

The entire kennel of dogs that fail to bark in this bill are all things AI. Despite some of the government’s late amendments sort of nodding, hinting, muttering towards this or, at times proxying, it is still extraordinary that, as AI features in so many cyber attacks, the bill seems so very oblivious to this. We tried.

We were also informed that a cyber bill was not the right place to put in the painfully overdue protections for our good-faith cyber professionals who do so much to keep us safe, often and understandably out of sight.

As the bill reappears in the Commons today, the immediate question is what the government will do with the amendments we got through in October. It’s safe to say that we will be seeing the bill again shortly and will continue to push on many of these issues.

Issues unaddressed

The CSRB will, eventually, receive royal assent, that is not in doubt. What is far less clear is how the raft of regulations will be brought in and at what pace.

With so many critical issues left unaddressed, there is one thing we can be clear on - the resulting Cyber Security and Resilience Act will have avoidably missed significant matters which would have made it far more coherent, created greater coverage and kept more sectors and more of us safe from the cyber onslaught.

Perhaps this bill, shortly to become an act, is not so much an iron dome - more an upturned colander?

title: Huang’s Trump-backed return raises AI sovereignty concerns
raw_text:
Just a week ago, during its third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia’s chairman described co-founder Jensen Huang’s behaviour as “inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms”.

Yet Huang is now back as CEO, thanks to US president Donald Trump’s direct intervention. His return leaves many questions unanswered, particularly relating to the influence of the White House on a private company and export controls and how these could be used by the US government to curb the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) acceleration technology in countries where it wants to exert influence.

During the earning call on 17 November, chairman of the board, Harvey Jones, said: “On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behaviour inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Huang’s departure saw the share price of the AI chipmaker plummet. His reinstatement led to shares in the company rallying.

Jones refused to take any questions regarding the former CEO during the call, but said the board acted deliberately and in the best interests of employees, customers, partners and shareholders. Yet just a week later, following what appears to be pressure from the White House, he said: “The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia , and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”

In a statement, Nvidia said that the board had received input from senior levels of the United States government and, based on that input, it was confident that Huang’s reinstatement would not pose a national security risk.

Huang’s reinstatement illustrates the strong links between the US administration and the chipmaker, and raises concerns over access to advanced AI chips should the White House choose to exert influence.

Forrester’s vice-president and group research director, Stephanie Balaouras, said the reinstatement of Huang as CEO may calm immediate concerns, but the concentration risk for businesses still remains: “The news changes the leadership picture, but not the strategic advice. The concentration risk still remains what it is.

“While Huang’s reinstatement may calm immediate concerns around Nvidia’s leadership, it should not reverse enterprise efforts to build alternatives into their AI infrastructure strategy. Restoring leadership does not mean restoring confidence in resilience. Leaders need to keep confronting AI concentration risk.”

It has been widely reported that Huang had an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore datacentre firm Megaspeed, which has been an Nvidia partner since 2023, leading to his decision to step down.

The Singapore link

Writing on LinkedIn, former US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) attorney John Reed Stark questioned the accuracy of Nvidia’s quarterly earnings filings. In the post, he pointed to the company’s fiscal 2023 filing through the first half of fiscal 2026. Stark said Nvidia’s annual report (10-K) and quarterly filings (10-Q) attributed roughly $52bn of revenue to Singapore, a city-state of about six million people.

“That total is my own addition to the figures in those filings,” he said. “Nvidia never published it as a single number. Nvidia explained in its footnotes that Singapore was mostly an invoicing address and that the chips went somewhere else. Then, one quarter after Nvidia reportedly put its largest Southeast Asian customer on an internal block list, the Singapore line disappeared from the filings altogether. The revenue did not. Nvidia had switched to reporting by customer headquarters, and the totals stayed the same.”

The US Department of Commerce began an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list.

Powerful AI chip restrictions

On 16 November, the US Department of Commerce department the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) published interim final rule entitled Addressing remote access to advanced semiconductors, which will require a licence to export, re-export or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil.

The interim final rule from BIS states: “You may not knowingly export, re-export or transfer (in-county) [advanced computer chips] for use in a datacentre to or within any destination worldwide that will provide access to more than 12 million aggregate TPP (total processing performance).” This TPP figure roughly equates to approximately 760 Nvidia H100 graphics processor units (GPUs).

While the restrictions do not apply to the UK, the Isambard-AI supercomputer in Bristol contains 5,448 Nvidia H100 GPUs integrated inside 5,448 Nvidia GH200 Grace Hopper, representing approximately 86 million TPP.

Commenting on the return of Huang, Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello said: “The company will face restrictions in selling leading artificial intelligence gear to countries (mostly in Southeast Asia) that were renting cloud workloads to Chinese AI model builders.

“The US government will undoubtedly have closer eyes on Nvidia, including a Securities and Exchange Commission accounting investigation. The US has made it clear that it considers Nvidia’s gear as a sort of weapon subject to regulation, and the firm will have to navigate this accordingly.”

Along with Alice Huang’s connection to Megaspeed, the US Department of Justice has been looking at whether she tried using US-based Super Micro to export servers equipped with AI acceleration chips indirectly to China.

title: Post Office to meet former subpostmaster over redress scheme disagreement
raw_text:
The Post Office has agreed to meet a former subpostmaster and his legal representative over concerns that redress schemes have not included potentially large volumes of branch losses.

Denis O’Donnell, who, for decades, ran a branch in Prestatyn, Wales, will meet the Post Office over his assertion that, despite promises, it has not properly alerted subpostmasters to an operational issue he first highlighted in 2019 that caused unexplained losses.

As a result, the former subpostmaster said that the closure of redress schemes means subpostmasters won’t be repaid the money they spent covering losses that were not their fault.

O’Donnell had originally informed the Post Office about a problem in 2019, but said he was “fobbed off”. But after pressure from Computer Weekly and forensic investigator Ron Warmington last year, the Post Office eventually investigated the issue and acknowledged it could cause unexplained losses.

Read more about O’Donnell’s revelation: Post Office scandal investigator warns public inquiry about Horizon defect at large for years

The issue, branded the “part payments” defect, was likely to have seen some customers, for decades, receive extra cash from subpostmasters without realising.

A Horizon screen icon that allowed subpostmasters to both take money and pay money was at the centre of the issue. When multiple transactions, including in and out payments, are held at the same time in what is known as a “stack”, Horizon could make a payment to the customer but record it as a payment to the branch, therefore creating an instant discrepancy.

In a push to get the Post Office to investigate further, O’Donnell will meet some of its executives, alongside Flora Page, a barrister who has played a central role in overturning wrongful subpostmaster convictions.

The Post Office confirmed the meeting but had nothing to add. It has previously said: “It is impossible to know the exact impact in the network [of the issue] and we acknowledge there will be subpostmasters who have experienced the issue and not raised it. But we do believe the overall impact is limited. The number of discrepancies in a year attributed to this process is 10 out of 14,000, or 0.07%, where discrepancies have been made known to us via our Review and Dispute button on Horizon.”

O’Donnell believes the Post Office is underestimating the issue. He said he raised the issue with the Post Office seven-and-a-half years ago, but it did nothing. He added that the problem had likely existed over a decade before he alerted the organisation. “I want the Post Office to fully admit to this problem,” said O’Donnell.

Page said: “It is encouraging that the Post Office has agreed to meet with Mr O’Donnell and me. We will have to wait and see whether they take appropriate action thereafter.”

It was after a 2018 High Court trial that the Post Office acknowledged it had wrongly blamed subpostmasters for account shortfalls caused by errors in the Horizon computer system and established its first redress scheme, known as the Horizon Shortfalls Scheme. Others have followed, including a scheme for those wrongfully convicted of crimes.

A scheme was later set up for subpostmasters who had experienced unexplained losses as a result of shortfalls caused by Post Office processes rather than computer-related errors, known as the Post Office Process Review (PPR).

This scheme was closed at the end of September 2026, despite calls from O’Donnell for an extension because he believed subpostmasters had not been properly alerted to an operational defect he identified.
